beats.narration_text: Hello, fellows. Faculty looked at the prerequisite graph and raised two things: a broadly useful chapter like Introduction to Cancer should show up in far more reading plans, and a single required-versus-helpful split wasn't enough. So this week I rebuilt the whole thing around three tiers, and I attached the real question bank to it. The question: how do you give a student a plan that's right-sized, strict where it has to be and generous where it helps, with a real question behind every step?

beats.narration_text: Every prerequisite link is now one of three tiers. Required: you have to know this. The target genuinely can't be understood without it, so these gate advancement, and they're kept strict and small. Recommended: you better know this. It strongly helps and you'll likely struggle without it, but it doesn't block, and this is where broadly foundational chapters live. And curious: aren't you curious about this. Related and enriching, but not needed, the lateral and synthesis links. Required gates, recommended helps, curious invites.

beats.narration_text: At the section level, that's one thousand two hundred eighty-three links: two hundred ninety-eight required, five hundred seventy-five recommended, and four hundred ten curious. Another three hundred two chapter-level links are derived from them. And it's clean: every prerequisite comes earlier in the book than the thing it unlocks, so the whole reading order has zero cycles. Appendices are left out entirely, since they're reference material, not steps.

beats.narration_text: Here's why a middle tier matters. Take Genetics and Genomic Instability. You can't understand it without basic cell biology, so Chapter one is required. But Introduction to Cancer is broadly foundational, it helps a lot, but you won't be lost without it. Under the old two-way split there was nowhere to put that. With three tiers it's recommended. And that one change is big: Chapter two, Introduction to Cancer, is now a prerequisite for a hundred and nine topics, almost all of them recommended.

beats.narration_text: Then I wired in the question bank. The questions are keyed to sections, so the whole thing chains together: a student's goal gives its prerequisites, the prerequisites give the sections, and each section pulls its questions. I mapped our collaborators' bank onto our sections and matched one thousand five hundred forty-four of one thousand five hundred eighty-four, ninety-seven and a half percent, about eight questions per section across a hundred ninety-three sections. Only five titles didn't line up, and those I'll reconcile by hand.

beats.narration_text: Put it together and here's what a student sees. Say the goal is immune checkpoint inhibitors, in Chapter twenty-five. The tool builds the plan: eight required readings as the backbone, eight recommended alongside, three curious, in reading order, each linked to its exact chapter and section with a reason, each tagged by tier. You can mark what you already know, or take a quick check from the real questions to skip ahead. And it's bounded: the required chain is taken in full, but recommended and curious hang off the goal rather than expanding forever, so a plan is about fifteen readings, not dozens.

beats.narration_text: What's honest about it. The three-tier graph is committed, the reading-order files are written, the questions are mapped, and the demo runs. And it's acyclic, verified, zero cycles. But every link is still a draft: provenance is llm-proposed or derived, needs-review is yes on every row. The questions come from our collaborators' bank, and five titles still need reconciling. So the structure is done and consistent, but not verified. The tiers, especially what counts as required, and the questions both need faculty.

beats.narration_text: So, where it stands. Three tiers, required, recommended, and curious, over one thousand two hundred eighty-three links, with zero cycles. A middle tier that finally fits the broadly foundational chapters. The question bank attached to the sections, nearly ninety-eight percent matched. And a bounded, tiered plan a student can actually follow. It's committed and consistent. What's left is the part only faculty can do: verify the tiers and the questions.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you're turning a dependency graph into a reading plan: don't settle for required-versus-helpful. Add a middle tier for the broadly foundational, and a light one for the merely enriching. Keep required strict so it can gate; let the rest guide without blocking. Attach your assessments to the same nodes, so every step comes with a way to check it. And leave an approve column for the expert.
